blocks.text: **Validity** and **truth** answer two separate questions. Validity asks whether the conclusion **follows logically from the premises**, so it depends on the **form** of the reasoning. Truth asks whether the statements **match the world**.
children: Validity is about form, truth is about the world.

blocks.text: The two can come apart. For instance, "All birds are animals, all animals have four legs, therefore all birds have four legs" is **valid**, but its conclusion is **false** because premise 2 is false. It would be a mistake to think a valid argument guarantees a true conclusion, and the reverse also holds, since an invalid argument can have a true conclusion.
children: A valid argument can have a false conclusion, and an invalid one can have a true conclusion.
Ask separately: does it follow, and are the statements correct?

blocks.text: In **modus ponens** you start with if p then q, affirm **p**, and conclude **q**. In **modus tollens** you deny **q** and conclude **not p**. Both forms are **valid**.
children: Ponens affirms p to get q, tollens denies q to get not p.

blocks.text: They are not judged equally, though. **97 percent** judged modus ponens correctly, but only **60 percent** judged modus tollens correctly, so tollens feels harder. For instance, "If I study I'll get a good grade; I didn't get a good grade; therefore I didn't study" is valid, even though it feels less natural.
children: Same validity, but 97 percent versus 60 percent correct.

blocks.text: Both valid forms were still judged correctly more often than both invalid forms. So tollens is harder than ponens, but it is not in the same trouble as an invalid form.
children: Valid forms beat invalid forms in accuracy, even the harder one.

blocks.text: **Valid forms** move from p to q, or from not q to not p. **Modus tollens** is the second kind, so it is valid. **Syllogism 3** goes from q back to p, which is **not valid**, and only **40 percent** judged it correctly.
children: Valid forms run p to q or not q to not p, never q back to p.

blocks.text: Going from q back to p fails because there may be other ways to get q. For instance, "If I live in Tucson I live in Arizona; I live in Arizona; therefore I live in Tucson" does not follow. The first premise says what follows from being in Tucson, and it does not say that Tucson is the only way to be in Arizona.
children: Other routes to q mean q cannot send you back to p.
The premise says what follows from p, not that p is the only route.

blocks.text: **Syllogism 3** and **syllogism 4** are both **not valid**, and **40 percent** judged each one correctly. They differ only in the second premise: in 3 it is **q**, and in 4 it is **not p**.
children: Same invalidity and accuracy; the second premise is what differs.

blocks.text: Syllogism 4 reads: if p then q; not p; therefore not q. The first premise says nothing about what happens when someone does not study. For instance, "If I study I'll get a good grade; I did not study; so I did not get a good grade" does not follow, because a good grade could come another way.
children: Denying p says nothing about q, since q can arise another way.

blocks.text: It would be a mistake to confuse these two with the valid forms that use the same premises.
children: Do not mistake an invalid form for its valid look-alike.

blocks.text: **Inductive reasoning** goes from observations to conclusions that are **probably but not definitely true**. Its strength depends on the **representativeness**, **number** and **quality** of the observations. For instance, many white swans support the expectation that the next swan is white, and one clearly observed black swan contradicts it.
children: Induction gives probable conclusions that new evidence can overturn.

blocks.text: **Deductive reasoning** asks something different, which is whether a conclusion **logically follows** from the premises. It does not ask whether the conclusion is probable. For instance, checking whether a conclusion follows from two premises is deductive, and the answer is valid or invalid.
children: Deduction yields valid or invalid, not probable.

blocks.text: Both versions of the Wason problem have the same **if p then q** form. In the **abstract version**, the cards are E, K, 4, 7 and the rule is vowel then even number. The correct cards are **E and 7**, yet **46 percent** chose the 4 and only **7 percent** chose the 7.
children: Abstract content: people mostly picked the wrong cards.

blocks.text: In the **concrete version** the rule is "If drinking beer, then 21 years old," with cards Beer, Soda, 16 years old and 21 years old. The correct cards are **beer and 16 years old**, and **73 percent** answered correctly. Familiar content calls up a **permission schema**, which makes the **falsification principle** easy to apply: look for situations that falsify the rule, and someone drinking beer while under 21 is the only case that breaks it.
children: Same logical form, but 73 percent correct with concrete content.
Falsify the rule by looking for the case that breaks it.

blocks.text: Context matters, but it would be a mistake to say familiarity alone is the reason for the improvement.
children: The permission schema, not familiarity alone, helps.

blocks.text: A **permission schema** is stored knowledge that if a condition is satisfied, an action may be carried out. For instance, being 21 is the condition and drinking beer is what can then be carried out. It leads you to check for anyone doing the action **without the condition**.
children: A permission schema tells you to hunt for action without the condition.

blocks.text: **Plain familiarity** is simply having experience with the content, and by itself it does not always improve reasoning. The improvement therefore does not come from familiarity alone. A permission rule is easier to reason about than an abstract rule about letters and numbers because the setting calls up the schema.
children: Familiarity alone is not the cause of the improvement.
The setting helps when it calls up a permission schema.

blocks.text: In the **gain frame**, Program A saves **200 for certain**, while Program B has a **1/3 chance** that all 600 are saved and a **2/3 chance** that none are. **72 percent** chose the sure A, a risk-averse choice. In the **loss frame**, Program C means **400 die for certain**, while Program D has a **1/3 chance** that no one dies and a **2/3 chance** that 600 die. **78 percent** chose the gamble D, a risk-taking choice.
children: Gain wording pushed people to the sure option, loss wording to the gamble.

blocks.text: Program A is the same outcome as C, and B is the same gamble as D, so only the **wording** changed (Tversky and Kahneman, 1981). In the gain frame people avoid the uncertain option, and in the loss frame they accept uncertainty in the hope of avoiding a certain loss. With 600 people expected to die, the same facts led to opposite choices.
children: Same facts, different wording, opposite choice.
Loss framing makes people accept risk to avoid a sure loss.

blocks.text: Under **opt-in**, you must take a step to be an organ donor, and consent is **under 28 percent**. Under **opt-out**, you are a donor unless you request otherwise, and consent is **over 99 percent**.
children: Opt-in gives under 28 percent consent, opt-out over 99 percent.

blocks.text: The easiest way to see the difference is to ask what doing nothing gives you. Doing nothing leaves you a non-donor under opt-in and a donor under opt-out. The **status quo bias** is the tendency to do nothing when faced with a difficult decision, so the **default decides the result**. The rates differ because of the default, and it would be a mistake to read them as a difference in underlying attitude.
children: Doing nothing means a different outcome under each default.
Status quo bias lets the default decide, not attitude.

blocks.text: **Expected emotions** are the emotions people predict they will feel about an outcome. They are predictions about the outcome itself. Kermer and colleagues (2006) studied predicted feelings about a coin flip.
children: Expected emotions concern the outcome being decided.

blocks.text: **Incidental emotions** are not specifically related to the decision. They come from disposition, recent experience or surroundings, and yet they still change the decision. Lerner and colleagues (2004) induced mood with a film clip. A person's general disposition also counts as an incidental source, so it can change a decision even when it has nothing to do with the choice.
children: Incidental emotions come from something unrelated to the choice.
Even unrelated emotions can change the decision.

blocks.text: Kermer and colleagues (2006) gave participants **$5** and a coin flip to win $5 more or lose $3. **Predicted feelings** were that losing $3 would lower happiness about **4 points** and winning $5 would raise it about **2**.
children: Predictions: a big drop from losing, a modest rise from winning.

blocks.text: The **actual feelings** were much milder. The drop from losing was about **1 point**, and the rise from winning about **1.2**. People overestimate the negative feeling because they do not consider the **coping mechanisms** that soften a loss.
children: The real loss hurt far less than predicted.
Ignoring coping makes a loss seem worse than it feels.

blocks.text: That feeds **risk aversion**, because people believe a loss will have a greater impact than a gain of the same size.
children: Overpredicted loss impact pushes people toward avoiding risk.

title: Sadness vs disgust: buying and selling prices (Lerner, 2004)

blocks.text: In Lerner and colleagues (2004), participants saw a sad clip of a person dying, a disgust clip of a dirty toilet, or a neutral clip of fish at the Great Barrier Reef, and then set prices for highlighters. The clips were unrelated to the choice, so these were **incidental emotions**, and they changed how much the same object seemed worth.
children: Unrelated clips still changed what the same object was worth.

blocks.text: **Sadness** lowered the selling price to about **$3.00** but raised the buying price to about **$4.50**. **Disgust** lowered both prices: selling about **$2.70** versus **$4.50** neutral, and buying about **$3.00** versus **$3.50** neutral. It would be a mistake to group the two emotions together, because they differ on the buying price.
children: Sadness raised the buying price, disgust lowered it.
Different negative emotions can push the same decision in different directions.

blocks.text: The weather is unrelated to the applicants or the school, but it still changed the decision. Incidental emotions include the **surroundings**, like the weather. Simonsohn (2007) analyzed admissions decisions.
children: Weather is an incidental influence on the decision.

blocks.text: On **cloudy days**, applicants' academic attributes were weighted **more heavily**, while on **sunny days** they were weighted **less heavily**. Simonsohn (2009) found that visitors to a highly rated university were **more likely to enroll** if they came on a cloudy day. These are not decisions about the weather, which is exactly why the effect counts as incidental.
children: Cloudy days increased the weight on academics; sunny days decreased it.
The weather changed the decision without being part of it.

blocks.text: Sanfey and colleagues (2003) had participants play **20 games**, **10 with each partner type**. The offers were identical, and only the partner changed. With a **human partner**, an $8 and $2 offer was accepted about **53 percent** of the time, and $9 and $1 about **37 percent**.
children: Same offers, different partner.

blocks.text: With a **computer partner**, the same offers were accepted about **85 percent** and **68 percent**. Participants became angry at unfair offers, and they were less angry with an unfair computer. Fair offers were accepted almost every time for both partners.
children: Anger at unfairness is weaker for a computer, so more unfair offers are accepted.
Fair offers were accepted either way.

blocks.text: According to **utility theory**, a **rational responder** should accept any offer, because even **$1** is worth more than nothing. Actual responders did not behave this way. They often rejected low offers, and participants with more **right anterior insula** activation rejected more, even though rejecting meant getting nothing.
children: Utility theory says accept everything; people do not.

blocks.text: In the game the proposer gets $10 and offers the responder a split, and if the responder rejects, neither receives anything. In Sanfey and colleagues (2003), fair offers of **$5 and $5** and **$7 and $3** were accepted almost every time, while lower offers were often rejected. **Emotion** is important in decision making, and it can lead people to give up money. **Neuroeconomics** combines psychology, neuroscience and economics to study this.
children: Rejecting is irrational by utility theory, yet common.
Emotion can make people give up money.

title: Decay vs interference as read from the Brown-Peterson task

blocks.text: Peterson and Peterson (1959) concluded that information **fades from short-term memory over time** unless it is rehearsed. They reasoned that counting backward is so unlike remembering letters that it should not interfere with them. That is the **decay account**.
children: Peterson and Peterson chose decay, with time as the only cause.

blocks.text: Keppel and Underwood (1962) offered the alternative, the **interference account**. Forgetting comes from other material getting in the way, as when letters from earlier trials compete with the set being tested. Both accounts explain the same result, recall that gets worse the longer the counting lasts, but they predict different things.
children: Interference blames competing material, not time itself.

blocks.text: Decay depends only on time passing, so the **trial history should not matter**. Interference depends on what else is in memory, so recall at the same delay should be **worse when more earlier sets have piled up**. That is the pattern in the trial-by-trial data, which points to **proactive interference** even though the original authors read the drop as decay.
children: Trial history separates the two accounts.
The trial-by-trial pattern favors interference.

title: Heard lists vs read lists (modality effect)

blocks.text: When items are **heard**, memory for the **last items** in the list is better, and the advantage also appears for lip-read or mouthed lists. When items are only **read silently**, the advantage for the last items is smaller. For instance, a list spoken aloud is remembered better at its end than the same list read on a screen.
children: Hearing boosts the end of the list more than reading does.

blocks.text: Neath and Surprenant (2003) tie the effect to extra information that comes with hearing, namely how the list sounded. The finding shaped ideas about **sensory memory**, because the end-of-list advantage seems to rely on a **brief trace of the sound**. The effect concerns the last items of the list, not the whole list.
children: A brief trace of the sound supports the last items.
The effect is about the end of the list only.

title: Sound code vs look code (Conrad, 1964; Murray, 1968)

blocks.text: A **phonological code** is a speech-based form of the items, so if items are held this way, **sound-alike** items are confused with one another. A **visual code** is a memory of how items look, so if items were held this way, **look-alike** items would be confused instead.
children: The code you hold items in predicts which items get confused.

blocks.text: Conrad (1964) and Murray (1968) found that **sound-alike lists were recalled worse**, even when they were read silently. For instance, the letters E and F look alike, but it was similar-sounding letters that were recalled worse. When **articulatory suppression** was applied to visually presented lists, the sound-alike cost disappeared, which shows people had been turning what they saw into a sound code.
children: Sound confusions appeared even for silently read lists.
Suppression removed the cost, so seen items were recoded as sound.

blocks.text: What matters is the code used to hold the items, not the format in which they arrived.
children: The holding code matters, not the input format.

blocks.text: The **phonological similarity effect** shows sound overlap hurting recall within the list. Items that sound alike are recalled worse because their **sound codes overlap** and get confused.
children: Sound overlap within the list hurts recall.

blocks.text: The **neighborhood size effect** goes the other way. Words that have many similar-sounding neighbors in the language are recalled **better**, because **long-term word knowledge** supports the short-term trace. For instance, cat is a large-neighborhood word and hippopotamus a small-neighborhood word, and Roodenrys and colleagues (2002) found large-neighborhood words are recalled better in short-term memory tasks.
children: Many neighbors in the language help recall through long-term knowledge.

blocks.text: Do not treat neighborhood size as another kind of sound confusion, since it is a long-term memory benefit. It also means memory span is not a pure measure of short-term capacity.
children: Neighborhood size is a long-term memory benefit, not confusion.

blocks.text: The **framing effect** is about how options are described. Choices change with the wording or context of equivalent options: gain wording leads people to choose the **sure option**, and loss wording leads them to choose the **gamble**.
children: Framing changes choices through the description of options.

blocks.text: The **default effect** is about which option is already chosen. People tend to choose the option that is preselected, whatever the wording. Giuliani and colleagues (2023) found that a **risky default raised risk taking**, a sure default did not raise risk aversion, and the framing and default effects were **additive**. For instance, a risky default raised risk taking on top of the framing effect.
children: The default works on top of the wording, not instead of it.

blocks.text: People who rated the default as most rational followed it most. That question came after the choice, so it does not show why they chose it.
children: The rationality rating does not explain the choice.

title: Unconscious attribute substitution vs error sensitivity

blocks.text: Kahneman and Frederick (2002) explain the error as **unconscious attribute substitution**. People answer an easier question in place of the one asked, for instance by overlooking the words "more than." This names a cause for the wrong answer.
children: Substitution claims a cause: an easier question replaced the real one.

blocks.text: Hoover and Healy (2019) prefer the term **error sensitivity**, because substitution cannot be confirmed as the cause. They checked what wrong reasoners remembered about the wording of the bat-and-ball problem (Frederick, 2005). Wrong reasoners **mostly remembered "more than"**, so the phrase was not simply overlooked, which counts against the idea that it was dropped.
children: Most wrong reasoners remembered the wording, against the dropped-phrase idea.

blocks.text: Error sensitivity stays closer to what was observed. It would be a mistake to say the study proved substitution, because it showed only that the cause cannot be confirmed.
children: The study did not prove substitution; it left the cause unconfirmed.

blocks.text: The **reward system** is the **ventral striatum** and **orbitofrontal cortex**, and peers watching can make these regions more active. The **cognitive-control system** is the **lateral prefrontal cortex**, which matures slowly and supports controlling impulses.
children: Reward regions drive wanting; the lateral prefrontal cortex supports control.

blocks.text: In Chein and colleagues (2011), adolescents watched by friends took more risks and showed more reward-region activity, while cognitive-control regions did not change with peers. For instance, an adolescent driving riskily when friends watch is explained by a more active reward system, not a less active control system.
children: Peers raised reward activity without changing cognitive control.

blocks.text: Albert, Chein and Steinberg (2013) read this as the peer effect working mainly through **reward circuitry** and not through weaker reasoning.
children: Peers push reward up; they do not lower control.

blocks.text: **Offloading** uses actions such as writing things down to reduce the mental load on memory, so the load sits **outside the head**. **Rehearsal** repeats information mentally so that it is not lost, so the load stays **inside**.
children: Offloading moves the load outside; rehearsal keeps it inside.

blocks.text: Morrison and Richmond (2020) found that offloading **improved memory**, especially at high loads, and that people offloaded more as the load grew. For instance, when they let people use pen and paper, memory improved most when the list was long. Memory ability did not predict who offloaded, so offloading looks like a strategy used across abilities, not only by people with weak memory.
children: Offloading helps most when the load is high.
Offloading is not just for people with weak memory.

title: Verbal vs spatial items under irrelevant speech

blocks.text: **Verbal items** can be named and held in a speech-based code, such as pictured objects. **Spatial items** are defined by where they are, such as dot locations.
children: Verbal items use a speech code, spatial items use location.

blocks.text: Leist and colleagues (2022) found that ignored speech **hurt serial recall of verbal items but not spatial items**, in both children and adults. For instance, third graders and adults were hurt on the objects but not on the dot locations. That fits **interference with phonological codes** better than accounts based on attention capture or changing-state speech.
children: Ignored speech damaged only verbal recall.
The pattern fits phonological interference, not general attention capture.

blocks.text: The speech effect is specific to verbal material, so it does not show a general loss of attention.
children: Not a general attention loss.

title: Falsifying a rule vs confirming it (Wason and Shapiro, 1971)

blocks.text: To **falsify** a rule is to choose the cases that could show the rule is broken. To **confirm** is to choose a case that can only agree with the rule and so cannot test it. A card that cannot break the rule teaches nothing, however well it fits, because the rule says nothing about what is behind it.
children: Only cases that could break the rule actually test it.

blocks.text: On the abstract rule, Wason and Shapiro (1971) found most people added a **confirming card** to the correct one, instead of the card that could break the rule. **Thematic rules** were much easier, because relevant experience helps people test them. A choice that agrees with the rule is not a test of it.
children: Abstract rule: most people picked a confirming card.
Thematic rules were much easier.

title: Younger vs older children and functional fixedness

blocks.text: German and Defeyter (2000) first showed children a box used as a container and then measured how fast they solved the problem. **Older children**, aged **6 and 7**, were **slower** afterward, so one shown use had locked the object in.
children: For 6 and 7 year olds, one shown use slowed them down.

blocks.text: The **5-year-olds** were not slowed, and were even **faster** than the older children after seeing the box as a container. The results suggest younger children have a **more fluid idea of function**, so one shown use did not lock the object in. This is **immunity to functional fixedness** in young children, though the finding is about speed after being shown a use, so it does not say young children never show fixedness.
children: Young children were not slowed by the shown use.
The claim is about speed after a shown use, not never being fixed.

title: Staying vs switching in the Monty Hall problem

blocks.text: **Staying** keeps the first choice, which keeps only the chance that the first guess was right, the **smaller share**. **Switching** wins the **larger share**, because the first guess was probably wrong and the revealed option removes a wrong one.
children: Staying keeps the small original chance, switching wins the larger share.

blocks.text: The first pick keeps its original chance, so the remaining chance moves to the one other option left. After the first choice, a losing option is revealed, and switching then wins more often than staying. Many people think it makes no difference, which is the intuition the problem is used to show is mistaken. It would be a mistake to reason that two options left means equal chances.
children: The revealed option shifts the leftover chance to the other door.
Two options left does not mean equal chances.

title: Percent correct vs the pattern of position errors

blocks.text: **Percent correct** counts only how many items were placed in exactly the right position. An item one place off counts as completely wrong, even though it still shows partial knowledge of its position.
children: Percent correct scores a near miss as a total failure.

blocks.text: The **position error pattern** looks at where the wrong items went. Items were usually placed correctly, and errors were **systematic**, with the item landing in an **adjacent position**. People keep approximate position information even when they miss the exact one, and a percent-correct score hides this.
children: Errors cluster near the true position.
Look at which errors were made, not only how many.

title: Self-report of imagery vs an imagery task (Shepard and Metzler, 1971)

blocks.text: Asking people to describe their mental images, a **self-report of imagery**, is unreliable, because you cannot tell whether the images or only the descriptions differ. An **imagery task with a varied critical part** avoids this problem.
children: Self-report cannot separate real image differences from description differences.

blocks.text: Shepard and Metzler (1971) had people judge whether two block shapes were the same or mirror images when one was turned. The **larger the turn**, the **longer the response**, at a **constant rate**. This suggests mental images are much like real images, because people **mentally rotate** them. The evidence is the pattern of response times, not what people say they see.
children: Response time rose steadily with the size of the turn.
Rotation timing is evidence for image-like representations.

title: Validity vs believability (belief bias and mental models)

blocks.text: **Validity** asks whether the conclusion must follow if the premises are true, so it depends on the **form** of the argument and not on what the words say. **Believability** asks whether the conclusion sounds true given what you know. These are separate questions.
children: Validity is about form, believability is about what you know.

blocks.text: **Belief bias** is answering the second question when asked the first, judging a syllogism valid because its conclusion is believable. **71 percent** judged invalid syllogisms with believable conclusions as valid. For instance, "All of the students are tired, some tired people are irritable, so some of the students are irritable" seems reasonable but is invalid. A believable conclusion does not make a syllogism valid, and an unbelievable one does not make it invalid.
children: Belief bias judges validity by believability.
71 percent called believable but invalid syllogisms valid.

blocks.text: The **mental model** approach (Johnson-Laird, 1999) is the safeguard. You build a model of the premises, form a tentative conclusion, then search for an exception where the premises hold but the conclusion fails. The conclusion is valid only if **no such model exists**.
children: Search for a counterexample model; valid only if none exists.

blocks.text: In the cesarean case, some physicians read the hypothetical test case **by itself** as the control. Others read the same case **after four cases** with serious complications, or after four fairly routine cases.
children: The identical patient was seen alone or after other cases.

blocks.text: **Significantly more doctors** recommended cesarean after reading the non-serious cases first. The cases just considered changed how the same patient was judged. Decisions depend on **context** and on how choices are presented.
children: Prior cases changed the judgment of an identical patient.
Context shapes decisions.

title: Emotion as a help vs a hindrance in decisions

blocks.text: **Emotion helps** decision making in a basic way. People with damage to an area of the prefrontal cortex who have **flattened emotions** have **impaired decision making**, so emotion takes part in decisions.
children: Losing emotion impairs decisions, so emotion is part of deciding.

blocks.text: **Emotion in excess** can lead to poor decisions. **Anxious people** tend toward risk avoidance, such as passing up choices that could lead to large negative consequences, and **optimistic people** ignore negative information. Emotions take part in decision making and do not only get in its way, and whether they help depends on how they push the choice. Emotion is not simply the opposite of good decision making.
children: Too much anxiety or optimism distorts choices.
Emotion helps or hurts depending on how it pushes the choice.

blocks.text: Both kinds of syllogism have **two premises and a conclusion**, and Aristotle introduced the syllogism. A **categorical syllogism** describes the relation between two categories using **all, no or some**, such as "All birds are animals, all animals eat food, therefore all birds eat food."
children: Both have two premises and a conclusion; categorical uses all, no or some.

blocks.text: A **conditional syllogism** has a first premise of the form **if p, then q**, where p is the condition and q is what follows. For instance, "If I study I'll get a good grade" is a conditional first premise. The conditional kind has **four types** that differ in the second premise, **two valid and two not valid**. A syllogism can be invalid even when every statement seems reasonable.
children: Conditional syllogisms start from if p then q.
Four types: two valid, two not valid.
